sections.text: You met the Göring Gambit sensibly: 2...exd4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.c3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 Nf6, and you got your pieces out with 6...Bb4 and 7...O-O. That gave you two pawns, while White had a lead in development.
White's 8.a3? was a mistake because 8.Nd5 was better. You hit back with 8...Bxc3!, which pinned the b2 pawn to the rook on a1, so after 9.bxc3 Nxe4 and 10...Nxc3 you were well ahead.
11...d5 gave you central control, and 12.Bxd5?? was a blunder as 12.Qxc3 was better. You took with 12...Nxd5 and kept developing with 13...Be6.
You then traded pieces with 14...Qf6, 15...fxe6 and 16...Nd4, and finished with 19...Qd2 and 20...Qxc1#. A very clean attacking game with 95.3 accuracy.

sections.text: Your opponent played the Center Game with 2.d4 and you accepted with 2...exd4, taking a pawn. White then tried 3.f4?, which was a weak move since 3.Nf3 was better.
You hit back with 3...d5 and after 4.exd5 Qxd5 you were a pawn up with an active queen.
5.Nc3? hit your queen but cost White more than it gained, since your queen could simply stay in the centre. You retreated with 5...Qd8?!, which was a small slip; the engine liked 5...Qe6+ better.
The game ended on time after only five moves, with you comfortably ahead.

review.turning_point: 3.f4? was the key mistake by White, because it gave you the pawn and the initiative.
review.focus: At move 5, 5...Qe6+ would have kept the queen active with check. Choose checks that keep your queen in the game over passive retreats like 5...Qd8.

review.headline: A solid game wrecked by two tactical oversights

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening where you got a decent position. 4.Bxe6 fxe6 traded bishops and gave you a half-open f-file at the cost of doubled pawns. 6...Nbd7?! and 8...Qe7?! were slightly passive, while 8.b4? was a mistake by White.
The pawn exchanges 10.bxc6 bxc6 and 13.dxe5 Nxe5 left the position about level. You had a playable middlegame with 11...Bh6 and 12...O-O.

14...Rac8?? was the real error. The d6 pawn was shielding your queen on e7 from the bishop on a3, so any capture by that pawn would open the diagonal. 14...c5 was the safe move. White missed 15.Qxe5 and played 15.h3??.
You then played 15...Nxe4??, when 15...c5 still fixed things. After 16.Qxe5 dxe5 17.Bxe7 the queens came off, but you were left behind in material and White won easily.

review.turning_point: 14...Rac8?? and 15...Nxe4?? both missed that the d6 pawn was shielding your queen from the bishop on a3.
review.focus: Before capturing or moving, ask which of your pieces is only defended by a pawn on the same line. At move 15, 15...c5 would have kept the position equal.

sections.text: You played the Bishop's Opening and 3.Qf3?! was ambitious. Black reacted with 3...d5?, and you took advantage with 4.Bxd5!, winning a pawn.
Several moves wasted some of the advantage. 5.Nc3? allowed 5...Be6?, and 7.Nd5? let Black trade bishops on d5. 5.Bxc6+ and 7.Bxe6+ were the cleaner choices.
9.Qc3? invited 9...Nxc2+??, a fork of your king and rook. But it was a blunder, because 10.Qxc2! simply took the knight and left you up a piece.

After 11.Nf3? and 12.exd5 Rxd5 you built a big lead, and 17.Bxe5 Qxe5 18.Nxe5 Rxe5 19.Qxe5 won more material. The record shows a draw even though the final position was strongly winning for you, so check how it ended.

review.headline: A Scotch where White threw away a piece and the queen

sections.text: This was a Scotch Game where you took the pawns correctly and traded on d4 with 4...Nxd4. White then blundered with 5.Be3??, which left you a knight ahead after the exchange. The engine wanted 5.Qxd4 instead.
You responded well with 5...Nc6!, moving the knight to safety while keeping the extra piece. You developed sensibly with 6...Nf6, which kept you around +3 for most of the game.

7...Ne5? was your only real slip, because 7...Bb4 would have kept the pin on the c3 knight and left White with a harder game. You stayed ahead and 9...h6! was a strong response to 9.Bg5?, asking the bishop where it wanted to go.
Then 11.Qg4?? hung the queen to 11...Nxg4!, and you ended up far ahead. The record lists this game as a loss, which does not match the board, so it is worth checking how it ended.

review.turning_point: 11.Qg4?? hung White's queen to 11...Nxg4!, and the position was completely winning for you by move 11.
review.focus: Your only real error was 7...Ne5?. 7...Bb4 would have kept the pin on the knight on c3. When you are ahead, trade pieces and keep your opponent's play restricted.
